paragraphs.source_en: A number of indicators from the archaeology, climatology and the rock art itself suggest that the most probable period of the Round Head origin was the 10th millennium BP. We also possess two direct dates from presumed Round Head paintings from the Acacus, both at 6th millennium BP (Ponti&Sinibaldi 2005; Mori et al. 2006). This chronological assessment would imply a four millennia long tradition of this art, and it would also imply that this art was in part contemporaneous with the Pastoral style attested in the region from 7,500 BP. The next section describes a possible evolution of the Round Heads during and after the arrival of the pastoralists, and it hypothesises what happened with both artistic traditions and their creators after the definitive onset of the arid climatic conditions.

paragraphs.source_en: Although the Round Head art is very homogeneous and conservative, it is believed that in its final stages it presents new elements and changes in style (Sansoni 1994; Muzzolini 1995a; Soleilhavoup 2007). Although the final stages have not yet been convincingly identified, there is, amongst all researchers, a presumed evolution from a simple into a more elaborated form which seems to be the decisive factor in establishing the Round Head final phase.

paragraphs.source_en: A careful examination of the presumed final figures in the rare cases of superimposition confirms that the more elaborated forms are indeed later than the simple ones. For example, at Techakelaouen in the Tassili simple Round Head anthropomorphic figures consisting of a red border filled with brown colour are superimposed by large sophisticated figures with bi-coloured body decoration and elaborated masks (Fig. 4-5). In the same shelter these later Round Head figures are superimposed by much smaller figures of the Pastoral period, showing a relative chronology. The main difference between the earlier and later Round Heads is in the representation of anthropomorphic figures. Whereas they were rather bulky with no facial features for most of the period, in the final stages they are much more elegant and realistic, with the nose and lips represented.
